title: Simple & Compound Interest
relevance: Campus OAs and aptitude rounds test SI/CI formulas, compounding-frequency adjustments, CI−SI differences, and present-value instalment setups.

phases.goal: Establish SI and CI definitions, amount formulas, frequency adjustments, and CI−SI difference formulas.

must_hit.point: Simple interest is SI = (P × R × T) / 100, and amount A = P + SI.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States SI = PRT/100 with P principal, R rate per annum, T in years, and A = P + SI.

must_hit.point: Compound amount after n periods is A = P(1 + R/100)^n, and CI = A − P.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes A = P(1+R/100)^n with R as rate per period and CI as A minus P.

must_hit.point: Half-yearly compounding uses rate R/2 with 2T periods; quarterly uses R/4 with 4T periods.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both adjustments: halve or quarter the rate and double or quadruple the period count.

must_hit.point: For 2 years, CI − SI = P(R/100)^2; for 3 years, CI − SI = P(R/100)^2(R/100 + 3).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls both closed-form difference formulas for the 2-year and 3-year cases.

probes: State the SI and CI formulas, how half-yearly and quarterly compounding adjust rate and periods, and the CI−SI difference formulas for 2 and 3 years.

hints.1: Separate what SI adds on principal from what CI multiplies each period.
hints.2: Write SI = PRT/100 and A = P(1+R/100)^n, then scale R and n for compounding frequency.
hints.3: SI = PRT/100 with A = P+SI; CI amount A = P(1+R/100)^n with CI = A−P; half-yearly R/2 and 2T, quarterly R/4 and 4T; 2-year Diff = P(R/100)^2.

phases.goal: Show how to compute SI/CI with fractional time, rate recovery, multiples, split lending, and interest-on-interest.

must_hit.point: Under SI, convert months to a fractional year (months over 12) before using SI = PRT/100.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Turns mixed years-and-months into a single fractional T, then plugs into the SI formula.

must_hit.point: If a sum becomes n times itself in T years at SI, it becomes m times in ((m−1)/(n−1)) × T years.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses linear SI: interest for n-times is (n−1)P in T years, so m-times needs (m−1)/(n−1) times as long.

must_hit.point: For 2 years at rate R%, the effective compound rate is R + R + R²/100 percent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Applies successive percentage change: two R% steps plus the cross term R²/100.

must_hit.point: For a fractional final year under annual compounding, compound full years first, then apply proportional simple interest on that amount for the leftover fraction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Finishes complete compound years, then multiplies by one plus the proportional rate for the remaining fraction.

must_hit.point: CI equals SI in the first year; from the second year, CI also includes interest on the first year's interest.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States year-1 equality and that year-2 CI adds interest-on-interest on top of another year of interest on principal.

probes: How do you handle fractional years under SI versus annual CI, and what is the SI rule for going from n-times to m-times?

hints.1: Ask whether interest is linear in time or applied to a growing base.
hints.2: For SI multiples use ((m−1)/(n−1))×T; for partial CI years, finish full compounds then apply a proportional rate.
hints.3: Convert months via /12 for SI; CI for 2½ years means two full compounds then half-year SI on the new amount; year-1 CI equals SI.

phases.goal: Contrast linear SI with multiplicative CI, when difference formulas help, and why instalments need present value.

must_hit.point: SI grows linearly with time on principal only; CI multiplies the running amount each period, so interest earns interest.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts PRT-style linear interest with A = P(1+R/100)^n multiplicative growth.

must_hit.point: The CI−SI gap is interest-on-interest; the ratio of 3-year difference to 2-year difference equals 3 + R/100, which recovers R without finding P first.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses D3/D2 = 3 + R/100 from the difference formulas to solve for rate.

must_hit.point: Equal annual loan instalments must equate the present values of each instalment to the original principal, not split the matured amount or subtract from principal directly.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes P = X/(1+r) + X/(1+r)^2 (or the analogous PV sum) instead of dividing final amount by two.

probes: Why does CI exceed SI after the first year, how can D3/D2 give the rate, and why must instalment problems use present values?

hints.1: Compare what each method does with interest already earned, and how future payments relate to today's principal.
hints.2: Difference formulas isolate interest-on-interest; instalments discount each future payment back to today.
hints.3: D3/D2 = 3 + R/100; instalments satisfy P = Σ X/(1+r)^k rather than principal/2 or final-amount/2.

phases.goal: Apply SI/CI to growth multiples, population-style problems, interrupted compounding, and phase switches.

must_hit.point: Under CI, if the amount multiplies by a fixed factor each block of years, total time is (number of such blocks) times block length — e.g. triple every 4 years to reach 81 = 3^4 takes 16 years.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Counts compounding cycles from the growth-factor power and multiplies by years per cycle.

must_hit.point: Population or similar percent growth is modeled like compound interest: past population = current / (1 + R/100)^n.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Inverts A = P(1+R/100)^n to recover an earlier population or balance.

must_hit.point: When a withdrawal interrupts compounding, apply interest to the current balance, subtract the withdrawal from that credited amount, then compound only the remainder.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks step-by-step: compound, withdraw from the post-interest balance, continue CI on what remains.

must_hit.point: A scheme can run an SI phase first, then treat the ending SI amount as the new principal for a later CI phase.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Computes SI amount for the first phase, then applies CI to that new principal for later years.

probes: If a balance compounds and money is withdrawn mid-way, how do you find the final value, and how do CI growth-multiple timelines work?

hints.1: Always operate on the running balance after each credit or withdrawal, not only the original principal.
hints.2: For CI multiples, write the target as a power of the per-cycle factor; for withdrawals, compound then subtract then compound again.
hints.3: If P→3P every 4 years and 81 = 3^4, time is 16 years; after a withdrawal, continue CI only on the post-withdrawal balance.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: SI = PRT/100 adds interest linear in time on principal only; CI multiplies via A = P(1+R/100)^n so interest earns interest. Over the same P, R, and time, CI exceeds SI after year 1; the 2-year gap is P(R/100)^2 and the 3-year gap is P(R/100)^2(R/100 + 3).

tradeoffs.topic: Full-year compounding vs fractional leftover year
tradeoffs.strong_answer: With annual compounding and a fractional final period, compound complete years first, then apply proportional simple interest on that amount for the fraction (e.g. half-year at half the annual rate), rather than treating the fraction as another full compound period.

tradeoffs.topic: Naive instalment split vs present-value instalments
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Equal annual repayments are not principal/2 or final-amount/2; equate the loan principal to the sum of discounted instalments so each future payment is valued in today's money.

gotchas.trap: In instalment problems, subtracting instalments from the principal directly or dividing the final amount by two.
gotchas.correction: Equate the present values of the instalments to the original loan amount.

gotchas.trap: Treating a mid-stream withdrawal as reducing the initial principal, or computing interest on withdrawn and remaining parts with mismatched timelines.
gotchas.correction: Compound step-by-step: apply interest to the current balance, subtract the withdrawal from that credited amount, then compound only what remains.

gotchas.trap: Assuming CI always differs from SI even in the first year.
gotchas.correction: CI for the first year equals SI; the extra appears from year 2 onward as interest on prior interest.
